synopsis: This review distinguishes two historical autosomal-dominant phenotypes. ADO1 was characterized by generalized osteosclerosis, most pronounced in the cranial vault, without an increased risk of fracture or osteomyelitis. ADO2 is most pronounced in the spine and long bones and carries an increased risk of fracture and of osteomyelitis, particularly of the mandible. Genetic testing later showed these are mechanistically distinct. Hematopoietic-cell transplantation is described as standard of care for infants with most autosomal-recessive forms, whereas data in autosomal-dominant disease are limited. Interferon gamma-1b is FDA-approved for severe infantile osteopetrosis, but the trials included too few people with non-infantile autosomal-dominant disease to show whether it works in that group.

teachingPoints.claim: ADO2, unlike ADO1, carries increased fracture and osteomyelitis risk, especially mandibular.
